analysis.title: Securitization Weekly Overview: AI and the household wealth accelerator
key_insights: BofA argues the roughly $196tn US household balance sheet gives the financial system the capacity to absorb $1-2tn of annual AI capex. Higher household net worth expands financing capacity through risk-bearing, collateral and portfolio reallocation. It does not create equivalent cash or saving.

The thesis extends the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist financial accelerator (1998) from borrower balance sheets to the ultimate capital providers (households). BofA states this is an application of the framework, not a result established by the original model or a fully tested academic model.

The conventional wealth effect (higher asset values lead to consumption) is likely modest because financial assets are concentrated in affluent households with low marginal propensities to consume. That concentration may strengthen the financing channel for AI.

Base case: AI-linked debt issuance of $722bn in 2026E, $984bn in 2027E and $963bn in 2028E across the subset of companies analyzed, against capex of $1,134bn (2026E), $1,685bn (2027E) and $1,861bn (2028E).

Real household wealth growth in Trump 2.0 through 2Q26 ran at 6.4% annualized, fractionally below the record of 6.45% in Trump 1.0 (rank 2 of 20 terms). Real S&P 500 appreciation of 14.5% annualized ranks first. BofA thinks Trump 2.0 has good odds of finishing first on real wealth growth.

BofA frames the administration's de facto economic objective as maximizing real household wealth growth over the four-year term, and reads many policy initiatives as supporting asset values and private balance sheets.

Scale illustration: a 1% reallocation of a $196tn household balance sheet is about $2tn. $1-2tn of annual investment in 2027-2028 is about 0.5%-1.0% of household net worth. BofA notes reallocation must still be matched by buyers, prices adjust, and much wealth is illiquid.

Only primary issuance counts as capital formation: buying new corporate bonds, committing to infrastructure funds or funding data-center loan vehicles finances new investment. Secondary-market equity swaps do not.
Tobin's q is a complementary channel: high valuations make issuance less dilutive and raise the incentive to invest. It does not show that the investment will earn adequate returns.

The collateral channel (Kiyotaki-Moore) is not dominant. FINRA margin debt is about $1.48tn, under 1% of the $196tn household net worth. BofA puts more weight on risk-bearing, reallocation and intermediation.

Why the AI cycle differs from the pre-GFC housing cycle: household wealth to home equity ratio is about 5.47 vs a low of about 4.4 in December 2005. Borrowers (corporations and investment vehicles) are mostly not the households that realized the gains. Funding goes to potentially productive assets. BofA cautions that leverage and valuation changes amplify gains and losses in both cycles.
Failure modes listed: profitability disappoints, financing outruns cash flow, collateral becomes correlated, leverage becomes central, and inflation and rates crowd out financing.
BofA is optimistic that AI companies will clear return hurdles and says drawdowns like the current market phase will likely be good longer-term buy opportunities.

Securitized products implication: constructive on high-quality securitized credit, but not unambiguously duration-positive, since a productive investment boom can sustain capital demand, nominal growth and real rates. Direct opportunities: data-center CMBS/SASB and ABS, power and utility financing, semiconductor and equipment financing, and bank or private-credit loans distributed through CLOs.
Household net worth grew about 12% y/y in 2Q26. Under the Rule of 72, that pace would double aggregate wealth in about six years. BofA calls this an illustration, not a forecast.

Weekly recap: broad credit weakness on fears that AI may keep some issuers from clearing profitability hurdle rates. BofA thinks the AI fears are overblown. It reiterates its call from two weeks earlier to Buy the Dips over the next 1-2 weeks and believes the bulk of spread widening is over.

Agency MBS: basis widened 1bp WoW. BofA turned basis overweight on 10/9, expecting easing rates and volatility to tighten spreads. It projects 2027 net issuance of $158bn and gross of $1.12tr. Housing forecasts: existing home sales -2.5% y/y, new home sales +0.5% y/y, home price appreciation about 1%.
Non-agency MBS: weekly issuance about $5bn, YTD $213bn. Non-QM cash-out loans look weak and caution on them is expected. HELOC/CES is attractive for convexity and higher GWAC.
CMBS: BofA is neutral on private label and agency CMBS, with $162bn of private-label CMBS in the pipeline through end-2026 and soft spreads expected through rate volatility.
ABS: one deal priced for $521mn in the week, YTD volume $328bn, full-year forecast $407bn. Spreads are expected to be rangebound but biased wider.
CLO: AAA spreads unchanged at 122, single-A to BB wider by 5 to 25bp with BB at 785bp. BofA prefers secondary BB. MTD issuance $9.7bn, YTD $134bn.

Weekly sector returns (10/15-10/22): fixed preferreds +6.00%, 30y UST +2.11%, 10y UST +1.04%, TIPS +1.00%, munis +0.84%, agency MBS +0.74%. S&P 500 -1.04%, leveraged loans -0.22%, HY -0.23%, BB CLO -1.02%. BofA reads this as a rates-driven rally, not broad risk-on.

10y UST yield fell to its 50-day moving average of 4.96% and BofA says the long-term uptrend remains intact. A drop to the 100-day average of 4.76% is possible near term, but BofA thinks declines beyond that are unlikely.
Hyperscaler spread index (BOAAIT) widened 15bp to a YTD high of 137bp. HY OAS widened 17bp to 228bp, IG OAS widened 3bp to 87bp, and the Bloomberg MBS index tightened 5bp to 36bp.

Spread per unit of spread volatility (5-year view): CCC US HY (9.6) and leveraged loans (9.1) rank highest. Loans and CLOs remain at the high end, which BofA reads as a continued relative value advantage.
Spreads for CMBX 18 BBB- widened 18bp w/w to 972bp (+411bp YTD) and CMBX 18 A widened 13bp to 366bp. CLO BBB- widened 15bp to 300bp. France 5y sovereign CDS widened 24bp to 103bp.
Leveraged loan CCC yield rose 99bp w/w to 30.5% (+982bp YTD).
Gross fixed income issuance is $9.2tn YTD in 2026 (ex-munis), up from $8.15tn YTD 2025. The 2026 forecast for total US fixed income issuance is $11.6tn.

risk_factors: AI profitability disappoints, earnings estimates fall, and household net worth and risk capacity decline just as issuers need more external financing.
Financing outruns cash flow: capex built at too high a cost, financed too aggressively or made obsolete too quickly.
Correlated collateral: public equities, private tech valuations, data-center loans and power assets all depend on the same AI demand assumptions.
Leverage becomes central if investment increasingly depends on borrowing against inflated assets.
Inflation and higher rates crowd out financing or raise the hurdle rate for AI investment.
Equity values can fall faster than housing prices, causing risk capacity to contract abruptly.
Data centers can be overbuilt, power contracts can embed optimistic demand assumptions, private-credit vehicles can use leverage, and technology collateral can depreciate quickly.
The tailwind from household wealth is limited because much household wealth is illiquid and reallocation requires counterparties.

tension_points.bull_case: A roughly $196tn household balance sheet, with a financial accelerator effect, gives the system capacity to absorb $1-2tn of annual AI investment. If investment is productive, future earnings and wealth rise and help fund the next round.
tension_points.bear_case: If valuations rise without matching expected earnings, the cycle depends on continued asset appreciation and becomes fragile. Leverage, correlated collateral and rapid obsolescence of technology assets could reverse the accelerator.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI revenue and productivity gains fail to justify capex, so earnings estimates and valuations fall and household net worth drops while issuers need more external financing.

tension_points.theme: Credit dip after AI profitability fears
tension_points.bull_case: AI fears are overblown, the bulk of spread widening is over, and credit spreads should retrace tighter as the 10y yield and MBS OAS roll over. BofA recommends buying the dips over the next 1-2 weeks.
tension_points.bear_case: The week saw broad credit weakness on fears that some AI issuers may not clear profitability hurdle rates. Hyperscaler spreads hit a YTD high of 137bp.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A decline in the 10y yield beyond the 100-day moving average of 4.76%, which BofA considers unlikely, or further hyperscaler and credit spread widening beyond the current YTD highs.
